Deep Brain Stimulation

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In 2010 we brought you the story of young Dakalo, a girl from rural Thohoyandu who suffered from an sever movement disorder called Dystonia. Tonight we revisit her to see how she is doing.

Unique Selling Point:
This is truly a feel good story of the benefits of Deep Brain Stimulation, the people who helped to make it possible and the results.

Summary:
Dakalo has lived with Dystonia since she was only three months old. She has never been able to eat, sit or walk independently. Dystonia can be described as an imbalance in the neurotransmitters leading to involuntary muscle contractions that force the body into abnormal, sometimes painful, movements and postures.
There are several treatments available for the movement disorder, one being Deep Brain Stimulation or DBS. In DBS therapy, a small pacemaker-like device sends electronic signals to an area in the brain that controls movement. Although DBS does not cure dystonia, it can help manage some of its symptoms and subsequently improve the patient’s quality of life.


Further information:
Our story:
We recap on the 2010 story of Dakalo. We introduce her paediatrician, Dr. Elsa Lubbe from the Steve Biko Hospital in Pretoria, who diagnosed Dakalo’s symptoms and was also instrumental in arranging funding for the operation. Through Dr. Elsa Lubbe, Dakalo got the best medical team on board lead by neurosurgeon, Dr. Pieter Slabbert from Netcare in Pretoria, who performed the DBS operation in 2010.
Several months after the operation Dakalo was able to eat a meal on her own and walk without adult supervision. Due to the severe degree of her symptoms she still has uncontrollable movements but to Dakalo she feels her life has changed for the better. Some days are better than others but in general she has improved and are able to function better after the operation.
Our story then track two more case studies, Rebotile from Bushbuckridge and Xolani from Groblersdal. Both are patients of Dr. Elsa Lubbe in Pretoria and have been treated by her over the last 2 years. Again it was dr. Lubbe who managed to source the funds and neurosurgeon to perform the surgery. Dr. Nico Enslin from the Red Cross Hospital in Cape Town performed the surgery on Rebotile and Xolani with huge success.
Rebotile, a teenager, is an orphan and lives with her aunt in Bushbuckridge in Mpumalanga. Rebotile's neck pulled to one side till she had the Deep brain stimulation therapy. Today she is almost 90% better.
Our last case study is Xolani, a lovely boy who recently turned 18. For the first time he is able to go to school and is very excited about his recovery.
This is truly a feel good story of the benefits of DBS, the people who helped to make it possible and the results.

Press Release:


NO PRESS RELEASE ISSUED.
In 2010 CB broadcast the story of young Dakalo Ndou, a girl from Thohoyandou who suffered from a rare disorder called Dystonia, that causes ncontrollable body movements. The only solution for her was Deep Brain Stimulation therapy to control the signals to the brain. We were in theatre with her when she underwent surgery. This is an update on Dakalo and we share the story of two more patients suffering from dystonia.

Script:


Deep Brain Stimulation
Duration: 8 minutes 20 seconds
Tx: 19 March 2017

STUDIO LINK: In 2010 we brought you the story of young Dakalo Ndou, a girl from rural Thohoyandou who suffered from a rare disorder called Dystonia causing uncontrollable body movements. The only solution for her was to receive Deep Brain Stimulation therapy to control the signals to the brain. We were in the theatre with her when she underwent surgery. Tonight we bring you an update on Dakalo and share the story of two more patients suffering from the dystonia.
_________________________________________________________________________

SCRIPT:

V/O Dakalo has lived with a movement disorder called Dystonia since the she was a baby. She has never been able to sit, eat or walk independently. Dystonia can be described as an imbalance in the neurotransmitters leading to involuntary muscle contractions that force the body into abnormal, sometimes painful, movements and postures.

Bongani: How does dystonia occur?

Dr. Elsa Lubbe: It is actually fascinating. We don’t really think, I stand here and I don’t really think what I am doing. But somebody with Dystonia, something becomes jumbled up and instead of having a smooth movement that stops and starts it all becomes twisted and they can’t stop it. Somewhere in that signaling part it goes wrong and that is in the deep part of the brain.

Link: There is no cure for Dystonia. Current treatments target specific symptoms, relieve muscle pains, spasms, discomfort and unnatural postures and no specific treatment programme is appropriate for every patient.

V/O There are essentially three treatment options for dystonia: oral medications, botox injections, and surgery.

V/O When Dr. Elsa Lubbe saw Dakalo Ndou for the first time in 2009 her body was riddled with spasms and involuntary body movements. She tried a combination of treatments but none were successful. The only option was Deep Brain Stimulation or DBS therapy.

Bognani Bingwa: What does DBS do?

Dr. Elsa Lubbe: The best way to explain it is that constant stimulation of those nuclei overrides those jumbled up messages so that all those jumbled up messages fall away and the signaling can come through.

V/O In 2010 Carte Blanche witnessed the Deep Brain Stimulation procedure performed on Dakalo by Dr. Pieter Slabbert and his highly capable team at the Netcare Hospital in Pretoria.

Up audio Bongani link...

V/O In DBS electrodes are planted on both sides of the brain and then connected to a neurostimulator. The neuro-stimulator contains a small battery and a computer chip programmed to deliver a specific electric current at a predetermined frequency and pulse rate to control movements.

Dr. Pieter Slabbert: At this stage she’s about, I would say, 10% better with tremor. But the fact that there is improvement shows that the operation went actually very well.

Nurse; What colour shirt is that lady wearing?

Dakalo: Blue

Nurse: It is blue?. Okay, good girl.

V/O It is now 7 years later and time to go and see how dakalo is doing at her home town in Thohoyandou.

Bongani: Dakalo, we last saw you in 2010, so we came to see how you are doing today. How are you feeling?

Dakalo Ndou: I am very fine. I think the operation did help a lot. It did help a lot.

Bongani: And some days are better than others?

Dakalo: yah. Some days I have pain some days I am fine.

Reversal Bongani: And what was it like before the operation?

Dakalo: Ah it is very hard because I could not sit alone with my mother. I was just sitting at home. I could not sit on my wheelchair. I could not do anything. I could not hold anything.

Dr. Lubbe: It is not that impressive for the bystander. She does not look well does she? The thing with Dakalo is that she is a unique case. She started to have dystonia when she was an infant. And what we have learnt is that the percentage of life spent with dystonic seems to be a determining factor.

V/O Dystonia is a very complex, and highly variable neurological movement disorder. Dakalo suffers from primary dystonia which is caused by an underlying genetic mutation. In primary dystonia there is no lesion in the brain and it rarely occurs in children under the age of 12.

Dr. Elsa Lubbe: To have primary dystonia starting in young childhood is a rare condition. They are talking about 2 to 50 cases per million.

V/O Dakalo is one of those rare cases. Since 2010 Dr. Lubbe has treated only two other children with primary dystonia, Rebotile Mokgalaka from Bushbuckridge and Xolani Masengo from Groblersdal who started showing symptoms at the age of 9.

Bongani: What was it like? What do you remember?

Xolani Masango: I remember sitting with my aunt. I was watching TV and my neck started twitching.

Bongani: And before that you were perfectly fine?

Xolani: Yeh.

V/O Xolani is a grade 10 pupil. His father passed away leaving his mother as the breadwinner. She is well supported by her family.

Thembisile Masango: He complained of a sore neck because it was always bent. We used cushions to support his neck for the trip to school to ease his pain. We took him to the doctor’s but there was no diagnosis. We took him to churches for prayers but there was no help. Xolani became worse.

Link: Because dystonia is a rare condition it is not easy to diagnose especially for doctors who have not encountered it before so you can imagine the frustration of any parent as they watch their child progressively get worse and nobody can tell them what is wrong.

Xolani: I was having seizures every day. I could not sleep for three days. I had to sleep with sleeping tablets and then it got worst. I could not even breath.

V/O Eventually Xolani was sent to Dr. Lubbe who diagnosed him with primary dystonia and knew the only solution for him was Deep Brain Stimulation therapy. She referred him to Dr. Nico Enslin at the Red Cross Children’s Hospital in Cape Town.

Dr. Nico Enslin: In the past 6 months before he went for operation he could not even sit unsupported any more. So there was a rapid change for a period of about a year when Xolani definitely had deterioration of dystonia.

V/ Soon after the operation Xolani’s tremors subsided and the doctors have hope for further improvement over time.

Reversal: Bongani: And now you are back at school living a normal life, what is it like?

Xolani: It is awesome because now I can play with my friends and stuff. It is life changing.

Dr. Elsa Lubbe: He sent me a whatsapp saying ‘doc I am all about my own business now’ and functionally that is wonderful!

Dr. Nico Enslin: Without DBS Xolani would have relentlessly become worsened to a point that he is completely bed bound and with the inability to eat. And children can die from it.

V/O For Rebotile, Deep Brain Stimulation therapy has made a world of difference. Before she went to Cape Town for the procedure with dr. Nico Enslin her neck was pulling severely to one side.

Bongani: Rebotile, how long have you had the problem with your movement with your neck?

Rebotile Mokgalaka: It’s almost 9 years.

Bongani: And when you had the operation?

Ribotile: It’s fine...no pain any more.

Dr. Nico Enslin: Everything went very well with her procedure. And within a few days after the procedure she could smile much more which is something she could not do before.

Dr. Elsa Lubbe: She is our poster girl in terms of outcome. When you look at her you don’t think anything is wrong her.

V/O Deep Brain stimulation therapy has given new hope to many children. Even when only a small percentage of change is noticeable in it means the world to them.

Dakalo: I felt like I am over the moon. When I am on my wheelchair I was so happy; when I held my phone I was so happy. I don’t know how to describe it. I was so much happy.
_______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

With broadcast delivery:

10 second:
It’s an incurable condition causing muscle spasms and tremors but with deep brain stimulation, these young patients have a fighting chance at a normal life

10 second:
This boy suffers from an incurable disorder leaving him trapped in his own body unable to control even the simplest of movement.

15sec:
Xolani suffers from an incurable movement disorder called Primary Dystonia: his mind is willing but his body does not obey. His only hope is a procedure called Deep Brain Stimulation therapy.

15sec:
Primary Dystonia is a debilitating disorder which causes muscle spasms and tremors, but doctors are beginning to change these young lives.
Dr. Nico Enslin: Deep brain stimulation is probably the biggest innovation in movement disorders treatment for the last 200 years.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In 2010 we brought you the story of young Dakalo, a girl from rural Thohoyandu who suffered from an sever movement disorder called Dystonia. Tonight we revisit her to see how she is doing.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This is truly a feel good story of the benefits of Deep Brain Stimulation, the people who helped to make it possible and the results.
metadata.Summary: Dakalo has lived with Dystonia since she was only three months old. She has never been able to eat, sit or walk independently. Dystonia can be described as an imbalance in the neurotransmitters leading to involuntary muscle contractions that force the body into abnormal, sometimes painful, movements and postures. There are several treatments available for the movement disorder, one being Deep Brain Stimulation or DBS. In DBS therapy, a small pacemaker-like device sends electronic signals to an area in the brain that controls movement. Although DBS does not cure dystonia, it can help manage some of its symptoms and subsequently improve the patient’s quality of life.
metadata.Further information: Our story: We recap on the 2010 story of Dakalo. We introduce her paediatrician, Dr. Elsa Lubbe from the Steve Biko Hospital in Pretoria, who diagnosed Dakalo’s symptoms and was also instrumental in arranging funding for the operation. Through Dr. Elsa Lubbe, Dakalo got the best medical team on board lead by neurosurgeon, Dr. Pieter Slabbert from Netcare in Pretoria, who performed the DBS operation in 2010. Several months after the operation Dakalo was able to eat a meal on her own and walk without adult supervision. Due to the severe degree of her symptoms she still has uncontrollable movements but to Dakalo she feels her life has changed for the better. Some days are better than others but in general she has improved and are able to function better after the operation. Our story then track two more case studies, Rebotile from Bushbuckridge and Xolani from Groblersdal. Both are patients of Dr. Elsa Lubbe in Pretoria and have been treated by her over the last 2 years. Again it was dr. Lubbe who managed to source the funds and neurosurgeon to perform the surgery. Dr. Nico Enslin from the Red Cross Hospital in Cape Town performed the surgery on Rebotile and Xolani with huge success. Rebotile, a teenager, is an orphan and lives with her aunt in Bushbuckridge in Mpumalanga. Rebotile's neck pulled to one side till she had the Deep brain stimulation therapy. Today she is almost 90% better. Our last case study is Xolani, a lovely boy who recently turned 18. For the first time he is able to go to school and is very excited about his recovery. This is truly a feel good story of the benefits of DBS, the people who helped to make it possible and the results.
